Orwell is a unique game, I don't even know how to classify it. You could say it is a child of point'n'click and 'choose your own adventure' games, wrapped in a UI and gameplay style most conductive to the topic it tackles. This is nicely complemented by an elegant, simplified graphical style that attempts to give a modern flair to everything and the 'metro' UI. The soundtrack does its job perfectly, mostly just playing in the background but taking the reins when a more dramatic situation comes along.

And those aren't that rare; while Orwell starts pretty slow and almost mundane, it makes sure to ramp up the pacing in the later episodes. The web of connections keeps growing, facts become too numerous to recount and the invasiveness of the system keeps on growing. In the midst of all that, all the benefits and dangers of mass surveillance are shown through actual story even instead of just... you know, reciting them here and there. 

This leads to a few glorious moments when it is easy to be drawn in, slap your knee and declare what just hit the fan. And that is a very valuable part of Orwell, one that bought me; it is easy to immerse yourself in the action. Characters are multi-faceted, decisions will have consequences and being the part of an otherwise soul-less system is a chilling, educating experience.

Hats off.

First it kept appearing in my queue, but I didn't think I'd be interested, so I kept ignoring it.  Next, I finally added it to my wishlist.  Where it remained for at least a year.  Then I finally bought it on sale with a bunch of other stuff so then it just sat in my Library for several months while I played the other stuff first.  Then, the first time I booted it up I just couldn't make sense of what was going on design-wise and I didn't have the patience to figure it out so it sat in my Library for another few weeks.  Finally, the next time I played it, it made much more sense and everything sort of 'clicked' for me.  Now I love it.

Gameplay, pacing, design, story plot, and music are all especially evocative of Introversion Software's excellent indie hacking game Uplink, without the frantic time-is-counting-down aspect of Uplink.  When I play Orwell, I feel like I'm playing Uplink, but it's much brighter and prettier and I'm more relaxed, lol.

I'm glad to see the developers continue to support this game with new episodes being released.  Since the game has no vocal acting and is a basic (but graceful) design, I imagine they could continue to crank out episodes relatively quickly if the demand justifies it.  Which is good because I want more.  The hallmark of any excellent game.

Orwell is a really impressive and thought provoking game. It puts you in the role of an investigator working for the government of The Nation to investigate suspected criminals by looking through their social media and emails, listening in on their phone calls and texts and even looking through their computers.

What I really liked about this game is how you can influence events in your role as investigator. The choice on what information you upload or don't upload can impact on how your handlers decide to react to certain situations or how to handle suspects. It does make you think twice about what actions you take as sometimes those decisions can have serious reprecussions.

I also found the games story quite gripping. Through your investigation you encounter various suspects and even though you never interact with them directly you still learn a lot about them. Their history, personality and whats going on in their life. It does a great job of showing how much of your life can be pieced together online.

Overall I found this game to be a really pleasant surprise and enjoyed it a lot.  If you like a narrative driven game where your choices matter then Orwell is well worth playing.

I don't typically write 'reviews' for games, but I find myself needing to write one here.

Orwell is more of a graphic/visual 'novel,' as in there's a lot of reading... or pretty much *all* reading. You're job as the 'investigator,' is to use the information presented to form a series of reports & profile... Which I promise is more fun than you'd think.

You'll be represented with choices which can affect the way the story flows. It's critical to read all the print, and re-read, and make sure you get all the possible information possible. 

Okay, the boring part is over.

The game follows the story of a bombing, and you're compiling the information related to it, and braching off extremly far in what is one of the best stories I've ever played. Within 10 minutes of playing, I was on the edge of my seat guessing as to what was happening, what was going to happen, who's really involved, etc. It's extremly fun to guess while you're playing, but expect a LOT of unexpected. 

Story: 11/10 Honestly my favorite story ever, extremly suspenseful and joyful, yet so rewarding! 

Gameplay Mechanics: 8/10 I ran into a small series of issues (EXTREMLY MINOR) where it took me several tries to drag the options into the profile of the people i was trying to profile. otherwise everything works amazingly well, although the mechanics themselves aren't overly "Special," more typical but used amazingly well.

Length: 8.5/10 As the story is good, the length did leave a BIT to be desired, but considering the cost of the game, and how rigerious game developement is, It's a good length. I clocked at 3.4 hours. A speed runner could probably do it in 1.5. I'd guess average would be... 2.5-3.

Price: 11/10 I'd happily spend more than the 10 i spend, I'd say easily 25. 

Overall, I love this game to pieces. #1 game on my steam list now, and I just purchased it's sequal. Yes, it has one. Yay!

Remember when we were all shocked by the Snowden leaks a few years ago? Ever wanna play at being the NSA trying to stop a terrorist threat?

PROS:
+Simple gameplay, but still fun.
+Take part in uncovering a deep and interconnected web of investigation.
+Lots of morally gray areas.
+Philosophically intriguing.
+Politically potent.
+While you investigate, you are sometimes forced to make decisions without a wider understanding, and hope you made the right call. It's crushing when you find out that you made a mistake.
+Excellent soundtrack!
+A calm, peaceful aesthetic clashes with the dark subject matter in the perfect way.
+Definitely rewards taking your time to read through everything going on, with lots of little tidbits to help tell the whole story. Worth additional playthroughs.
+A world which feels truly lived-in, from the news to the social media to the characters.
+Your choices matter, and there's multiple, distinct endings which feel different from eachother when you look at the end result.

CONS:
-Only 3 hours to beat my first playthrough, then another 3.5-5 hours to get all of the achievements. Sadly short, but at least there's a sequel.

Play the demo before you buy, as the first day is fairly reflective of the rest of the game. But I do strongly recommend this to anyone interested in this sort of subject matter.

In Orwell you sit in front of a virtual computer screen and attempt to track down the perpetrators of a recent bombing in an authoritarian surveillance state (hence the name of the game).

Set in the fictitious country of The Nation, you play The Investigator, someone employed from outside The Nation to work on its secret interior security project called Orwell. You receive verbal communiques one-way from your supervisor, who directs you on what to do. In return you send back snippets of information you find online.

In the aftermath of a bombing in Freedom Plaza (ironic name, geddit?), you must track down the perpetrators. You start from a single person arrested at the scene, and trace out her social and familial connections to bring more and more people under scrutiny. 

The Orwell computer system allows you to potentially pry into all aspects of a character's online life, as long as you can find a link to enable you to uncover each new aspect. You can look through public websites, but also snoop on messaging conversations, phone calls and email, as well as later being able to access the characters' computers themselves and have a nose around.

Certain information you come across is highlighted, what the game calls "data chunks", and you either provide these to your supervisor, or withhold them, to build a profile on someone and direct the security services to a conclusion about their guilt or innocence in the bombing.

It's a reasonable idea. However, to progress in the game, you have to throw out any common-sense notions you might have about how the information you provide will be interpreted, because it frequently defies any sense. 

The game makes it clear in the beginning that many of the "data chunks" are understood by your supervisor in their full context, but then all of a sudden something you pass along about a character referring jokingly to the "torture" of being dragged on a night out by a friend is taken completely out of context as referring to literal torture. The game tells you that information "uploads" into Orwell cannot be undone, but they also cannot be clarified.

Some "data chunks" are highlighted in a different colour, which you learn means that it conflicts with at least one other piece of information out there in cyberspace. You are only allowed to upload one of these pieces of information into the system, because it is a necessary game mechanic that the investigators cannot handle two or more possibilities for a biographic detail, so you have to pick one to send along. 

Someone might say that is how it is supposed to be, but these things feel forced as you play the game. It is especially frustrating because you often do not get any indication as to how each piece of information you decide should be taken for granted will affect what happens next.

Game events are seemingly triggered by your uploading information. This puts you in the position of uploading information you thought extraneous, or otherwise wished to withhold, in an effort to get the game to advance by finding the right trigger.

In the final act, you see written in what characters have said choices for an outcome. However, it is not clear how you are supposed to enact what I imagine for most players would be the desired outcome, nor does the character's explanation of how that outcome shall come about make sense.

Despite all of the references to Orwell's 1984, the comparison between The Nation and Oceania would be a lazy one. This is a game to suit someone who has only heard of 1984, and not actually read it. Where the extent of their understanding of the work is that that Big Brother fellow liked his surveillance. 

In the game, The Nation is authoritarian, but non-ideological. There is something about it being pro-interventionist and anti-immigration, but this does not serve as an effective allegory about real-world politics. Although the beastly Orwell programme reaches far into people's private lives, its administrators are awfully concerned with ethics and the rule of law. They have to gain legal warrants to bring someone under the scrutiny of the system, and are annoyed by your giving them extraneous personal detail. 

Although some important legal protections for the accused are absent, accused people are apparently entitled to legal representation. There is no indication that the state much cares about what people think, or that it coerces them into changing. That is, there are no thought crimes in The Nation, and state power is not arbitrary or lawless. Rather, its inhabitants appear to have have freedom of speech, thought and assembly (and, it seems from one plot point, the right to bear arms).
Fantastic.

"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" presents a haunting glimpse into the reality of a far too realistic surveillance state. It shows the importance of independent, critical thinking and the context of any tidbit of information.

This game provides a chilling experience through its compelling narrative. The interface is slick and allows easy immersion in the world of Orwell, where all information is at your fingertips and interpretation of every word in your hand.

I was looking for a different genre of game and bought Orwell when it was on sale thinking I couldn't do much wrong purchasing it. And the game delivered. It was exactly [u]what I was looking for in terms of theme and mechanics[/u]. It's a [b]short game (5 hours)[/b] and it's so different from the other 'typical' games, which makes it in my opinion very interesting.

I do think the game has some [u]negative points[/u] though, particularly in the fact that I felt obliged to follow a certain path of actions if I wanted to advance in the game, which didn't give me the choice I thought I would have. Although, there should be different endings and all depending on your course of actions, it felt more like I was still in a kind of tutorial mode choosing things I didn't want to in order to advance or else I seemed to be blocked.

Maybe a bit of irony there... Me, wishing I have freedom in a game that's all about controlling society.

Anyways, I recommend this game but buy it on sale because for the length of the game I don't think you should spend too much on it. I might probably give it another playthrough to try and find out the other course of actions.
